title: Rising demand for nuclear fuels: security, supply and the AI power boom
gist: Wood Mackenzie's base case has global installed nuclear capacity more than doubling by 2060 on AI/data-centre-driven demand for firm 24/7 power, creating a US$3.1 trillion investment opportunity, with lifetime extensions and restarts carrying the load through 2035. Much of the piece is a gated teaser for the 'Global nuclear fuel strategic planning outlook 2026' report, so the specific bottleneck answers are withheld — but the stated thesis is that fuel-cycle access, not raw availability, becomes the binding constraint as geopolitics reshapes trade flows.

themes.theme: AI-driven nuclear demand and the capacity outlook

insights.claim: Under Wood Mackenzie's base case, global installed nuclear capacity will more than double by 2060, driven by electrification, data centre demand and energy security concerns.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: A doubling over 35 years is the anchor assumption behind uranium and fuel-cycle demand models — aggressive versus history but not a step-change per year.
insights.quote: global installed nuclear capacity will more than double by 2060 on the back of electrification, data centre demand and energy security concerns
insights.locator: Nuclear investment is beginning to take-off

insights.claim: Doubling global nuclear capacity by 2060 represents a US$3.1 trillion investment opportunity as existing fleets expand and dozens of additional countries pursue commercial nuclear power.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable market for reactor vendors, EPC contractors and fuel-cycle firms — a concrete number to test equity valuations against.
insights.quote: creating a US$3.1 trillion investment opportunity as existing fleets expand and dozens of additional countries pursue commercial nuclear power
insights.locator: How much investment will be needed?

insights.claim: The governments of more than 70 countries are considering new commercial reactors, widening the range of nuclear technologies being pursued.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Demand is broadening geographically well beyond the incumbent operators, which favours exporters of standardised and small modular designs.
insights.quote: with the governments of more than 70 countries considering new commercial reactors
insights.locator: Nuclear investment is beginning to take-off

insights.claim: The nuclear industry's expansion is being pulled by AI-driven demand for firm 24/7 power rather than by conventional load growth alone.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Nuclear's investment case is now levered to AI capex cycles — a hyperscaler spending pause is a nuclear demand risk, not just a semiconductor one.
insights.quote: The nuclear industry is set for rapid expansion as the desire for firm 24/7 power grows as a result of the AI boom.
insights.locator: The nuclear industry is set for rapid expansion

themes.theme: Two-phase build: extensions now, new build after 2035

insights.claim: Through 2035, reactor lifetime extensions and plant restarts — not new construction — will be the mechanism used to meet short-term data centre power demand.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: The next decade's nuclear investable exposure is existing-fleet operators and restart candidates, not new-build developers whose revenue sits beyond 2035.
insights.quote: Through 2035, reactor lifetime extensions and restarts will be used to meet short-term power demand from data centres.

insights.claim: After 2035, growth in both conventional and next-generation nuclear is expected to be driven by standardisation, factory manufacturing and smoother licensing frameworks.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: The post-2035 case rests on cost-curve mechanisms that have never yet been demonstrated at scale in Western nuclear — the key falsifiable assumption.
insights.quote: with standardisation, factory manufacturing and smoother licensing frameworks helping to drive fleet expansion

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie leaves open how quickly next-generation nuclear technologies can move from demonstration projects to large-scale deployment.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Even the bull-case author will not commit to advanced-reactor timing — treat SMR deployment schedules in company guidance with heavy discount.
insights.locator: But how quickly can next-generation technologies move

insights.claim: Today's nuclear fuel market appears relatively well supplied, but that picture changes as deployment accelerates — capacity exists across much of the fuel cycle while geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and regional concentration make access as important as availability.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Physical adequacy is the wrong metric; price and security premia will be set by who is allowed to buy from whom, favouring Western-aligned conversion and enrichment assets.
insights.quote: geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and regional concentration mean access is becoming just as important as availability
insights.locator: Will fuel supply chains become the biggest constraint?

insights.claim: Parts of the nuclear fuel supply chain could tighten significantly during the 2030s as demand accelerates, particularly if geopolitical tensions continue to reshape global trade flows.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: The squeeze is a 2030s event, not imminent — argues for accumulating fuel-cycle exposure ahead of a tightening that current spot markets do not price.
insights.quote: some parts of the supply chain could tighten significantly during the 2030s as demand accelerates
insights.locator: Where are the biggest bottlenecks likely to emerge?

insights.claim: Nuclear fuel production remains concentrated in a relatively small number of countries, and long development timelines make it difficult for new capacity to come online quickly.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Supply inelasticity plus concentration is the classic setup for violent price moves on any single-country disruption in the fuel cycle.
insights.quote: Production remains concentrated in a relatively small number of countries, while long development timelines make it difficult for new capacity to come online quickly.
insights.locator: Where are the biggest bottlenecks likely to emerge?

themes.theme: New fuel types and strategic state intervention

insights.claim: Emerging fuels including HALEU, TRISO, thorium-based fuels, molten salt fuels and accident-tolerant fuels will require dedicated manufacturing capacity and entirely new supply chains as the reactor technologies using them mature.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Advanced reactors carry an unbuilt fuel-chain liability — greenfield HALEU and TRISO fabrication is a distinct investment theme from uranium itself.
insights.quote: Emerging fuels such as HALEU, TRISO, thorium-based fuels, molten salt fuels and accident-tolerant fuels are expanding the range of reactor technologies under development.
insights.locator: Which nuclear fuels will shape the next generation of reactors?

insights.claim: Governments are increasingly treating advanced nuclear fuel production as a strategic priority to improve energy security and reduce reliance on existing suppliers, and are both supporting production and restricting exports.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Expect state subsidy on the build side and export controls on the trade side — a policy-supported margin for domestic fuel-cycle champions.
insights.quote: geopolitical and energy security concerns are prompting governments to support increased nuclear fuel production and restrict exports
insights.locator: The big question is whether the supply chain will be ready

insights.claim: Private capital from AI hyperscalers is injecting innovation and scale into the nuclear fuel market, an unusual funding source for a historically state-and-utility-financed industry.
insights.speaker: Prakash Sharma
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler balance sheets can de-risk fuel-chain projects that utilities would not fund — watch for offtake and equity deals as the leading signal of real capacity.
insights.quote: Private capital from AI hyperscalers is injecting innovation and scale into the market.
insights.locator: The big question is whether the supply chain will be ready
